label: Postgres: Query
description: Run SQL against Postgres and get the rows back. Parameters are the node's own inline-declared input ports, read by name: `PostgresExecuteQuery(userId: String) { query: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $userId" }`; the build fails on a `$name` that is no input of the node, and on an input the query never uses. Binding: a string as the text of the placeholder's type (so `$when::timestamptz`, a uuid column or `$amount::numeric` parse it like a quoted literal), a boolean as bool, a number to whatever numeric column it meets, null anywhere, an object or list as jsonb where the placeholder is json or jsonb (`$params::jsonb->>'id'`) and as its JSON text elsewhere, so a list of numbers writes a pgvector `vector` or `halfvec` column. Where Postgres cannot infer a parameter's type (inside `jsonb_build_object(...)`, `$x IS NULL`, bare `SELECT $x`) it refuses with "could not determine data type of parameter": cast it (`$x::text`). A port used twice is ONE parameter with one type, so `'...' || $id` makes `id` text and a uuid or integer comparison on it then fails; use a separate port. Several statements form a script: with `$name` parameters they run in one transaction, each with the ports it names; without any, all but the last run whole (transaction control and utility statements work) and the last runs alone. To change a table a live program is using (an `ALTER TABLE`, a `CREATE INDEX`), start the query with `SET lock_timeout = '5s';`: the change then fails after 5 seconds instead of waiting behind the queries holding the table, with every new query on that table queued behind it; it works in either kind of script, and the setting ends with the run. A `vector` or `halfvec` column comes back as a list of numbers; a column of a type the node cannot read (`sparsevec`, `point`, ...) refuses the query before it runs, so cast it (`weights::text`). The last statement's rows come back: all of them on `rows` (`[]` when none), the first on `row`. To have them checked, declare their shape in the program, `type User = { id: String, name: String | Null, .. }`, and on the node `-> (row: User)` or `-> (rows: List[User])`: a row that does not fit fails the node naming the field (catchable by `_error`). `..` ignores the columns the type does not name; a column that can be NULL is typed `T | Null`. With no rows `row` closes, so whatever reads it skips; declared `-> (row: User | Null)` it carries `null` instead. To fail on purpose, define once in the schema `CREATE FUNCTION fail(msg text) RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION '%', msg; END $$;` and call `SELECT fail('no such publication') WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)` (a `$port` inside a `DO` body is plain text, not a parameter). A data-modifying CTE (`WITH ins AS (INSERT ... RETURNING *) SELECT ...`) is invisible to the rest of its statement: read from `ins`, not the table. Unreachable database, a connection lost mid-query (noticed about a minute after the server stops answering), broken constraint, `fail(..)` or missing privilege: catchable by `_error`. So are rows weighing more than 100 KB in all, the most a wire carries: page a big result with `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`. An SQL mistake (syntax, unknown table or column, positional `$1`): always fails the run.

inputs.name: account
inputs.description: Wire a PostgresAccess, or a PostgresDatabase's access output.

inputs.name: query
inputs.label: SQL
inputs.description: The SQL; each `$name` reads the inline-declared input port of that name.

outputs.name: rows
outputs.description: Every row the query answered (the last statement's, for a script), keyed by column; `[]` when none. Declare `-> (rows: List[User])` to have each row checked against `User`.

outputs.name: row
outputs.description: The first row, the same as the first of `rows`. Closes when the query answered none; declared `-> (row: User | Null)` it carries `null` instead.

outputs.name: count
outputs.description: Rows RETURNED (length of `rows`), not rows changed: a plain INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE gives 0; add `RETURNING id` to count them.

then.message: '{id}' wires `count`, but its statement answers no rows: `count` is how many rows came BACK, not how many a write changed, so it would be 0 on a write that worked perfectly and anything gated on it would never fire. Add `RETURNING id` (or whichever column) to the statement, and `count` becomes the number of rows it touched.
